rv.q: Diamond was a kind of talisman, and his music, filled with his signature blend of macho groan and sweet melodiousness, is complex enough to stand a show like this.
That fits him, and his musical of the same name, like a hand in a glove.
By that point it feels rushed and not quite earned, not to mention a little too nakedly sentimental.
In the end, A Beautiful Noise can't overcome the central challenge of being a Neil Diamond biomusical, which is that Diamond's life has not been, in and of itself, especially dramatic.
But while the show moves briskly, dodging the story’s gloom-ridden banality proves impossible.
The thing is, there’s just not much of a show there.
Unexplored holes like these riddle the script, which is desperate for more of Diamond’s insides, but “A Beautiful Noise” is a bio-musical that has forgotten the first half of its form.
Just something to help lubricate one of the most puzzling jukebox musicals in years.
But “A Beautiful Noise” is one off-key moment after another.
And whatever else you might say about Neil Diamond, he certainly had a way with a catchy tune.
'A Beautiful Noise' manages to fly on the strength of the collective talent behind it, not least of all Mr. Diamond's.
Everything that works does it so well but the aspects that don’t are the typical traps of a bio- or jukebox musical, cheapening the overall experience.

Will Swenson, the charismatic star of "A Beautiful Noise," is hampered by the full-steam-ahead pacing of the show, leaving little time for introspection. He is a powerhouse, molding his voice to sound like the actual Neil Diamond as best he can, often missing the mark.
Sadly, it’s not, but it’s a mostly enjoyable outing thanks largely to Swenson’s impeccable characterization and the songwriter’s enduring brilliance.
If you are looking for life changing theatre you can look elsewhere.
Those going to A Beautiful Noise want to be entertained and entertained they will be.
Despite being a lukewarm look at the Brooklyn-born superstar, the show headlined by Will Swenson will nonetheless appeal to Diamond’s ardent fans.
For now, though, Swenson & Co. offer a reasonable facsimile of Diamond in the flesh for fans to soak up.
Yet I found “A Beautiful Noise: The Neil Diamond Musical” less engaging than “Beautiful: The Carole King Musical.”

However, O’Connell is such a good, transporting actor that even as the drama on stage barrels into cuckoo-land, she grounds it and the audience with Becky’s quirkiness, passion, fierceness, and laughter.
Even better news: Will Swenson (Hair, Priscilla: Queen of the Desert) is sensational as the guitar-strumming, chart-topping, stadium-playing young Diamond.

While A Beautiful Noise isn’t quite as weak as some have made it out to be, when compared to other recent shows with similar ambitions, like those about Carole King, the Temptations, Michael Jackson, and Tina Turner, this remains an undistinguished contribution.
The problem is that Diamond, at least as he’s portrayed here, isn’t much fun to spend two-and-a-quarter hours with.
With that in mind, I would have preferred a karaoke bar where everyone gets drunk and sings along to Diamond’s greatest hits over “A Beautiful Noise.”
Well, there were times I forgot about the show as I sat there watching it.
Sometimes songs are force fed to move the action.
For Diamond fans A Beautiful Noise is a love letter and a bounteous gift of musical exultation, with enough juice to welcome a non-boomer audience into the cult of Diamond.

cn.t: Critics find this Neil Diamond biomusical a formulaic crowd-pleaser that delights fans with energetic performances of beloved hits, but suffers from a weak therapy-framed book and tonally confused storytelling.

vs.sum: One of Broadway's least comfortable theaters, with notoriously tight legroom and narrow seats. The lack of rake means tall patrons in front block your view. Restrooms are in the basement, creating long intermission lines. For legroom, target Row A or N in Orchestra.

acc.note: 6 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. No steps from sidewalk. Infrared devices available.
